title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 101: Notice of meeting

content.overview: Section 101 ordinarily requires clear 21 days’ notice of a general meeting, specifies what the notice must state and identifies the persons entitled to receive it. Shorter notice is possible only with the consent specified by the section.
content.glance: Give clear 21 days’ notice. Shorter notice needs written/electronic consent: 95% of members entitled to vote for an AGM; for another meeting, majority in number plus 95% voting share capital, or 95% voting power without share capital. This section does not apply to an OPC: see section 122(1) and its separate procedure.
content.study:
## Notice period and shorter notice
A general meeting may ordinarily be called by giving not less than clear 21 days’ notice in writing or through the prescribed electronic mode. Under the proviso substituted by section 28 of the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017, shorter notice requires written or electronic consent on different tests: (i) for an annual general meeting, not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote at it; and (ii) for another general meeting, where the company has share capital, a majority in number of members entitled to vote who represent not less than 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying a right to vote at the meeting; or, where the company has no share capital, members holding not less than 95% of the total voting power exercisable at the meeting. A further proviso requires a member who can vote only on some resolutions to be counted only for those resolutions. Do not apply the AGM test automatically to an EGM.

## Contents and recipients
The notice must specify the place, date, day and hour of the meeting and state the business to be transacted. Notice must be given to every member, the legal representative of a deceased member or assignee of an insolvent member, the auditor(s), and every director. An accidental omission to give notice, or non-receipt by an entitled person, does not by itself invalidate proceedings under section 101(4); that limited rule is not a general cure for deliberate or material non-compliance.

## Electronic notice — Rule 18
Where the company uses electronic notice, rule 18 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014 supplies additional process requirements. The reproduced rule text addresses sending notice to the email address recorded by the company or depository; giving members without a recorded address an advance opportunity at least once in each financial year to register or update it; a subject line identifying the company, meeting type, place and date; non-editable attachments or an accessible link with instructions; retention of dispatch, recipient and failed-transmission/resending records as proof of sending; and ensuring linked material is readable and can be obtained and retained by the recipient. The reproduced rule also addresses when transmission satisfies the company’s obligation and the effect of a member failing to provide/update an address. The official G.S.R. 560(E), 13 June 2018, notification separately confirms that the Explanation after rule 18(3)(ix) was omitted. This establishes that specific deletion only; it does not verify the full consolidated current Rule 18 or every amendment. This is a rule-level checklist, not a substitute for checking the remaining official Gazette text and any applicable meeting-specific rules or exemptions.

## Practical verification
Preserve the notice, dispatch/service evidence, recipient list, consent records, voting entitlement by resolution, and meeting particulars. Check the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, applicable exemptions, articles and any special provision governing the meeting. The current shorter-notice test must be read with the 2017 amendment, not solely from an unamended reproduction of the 2013 Act.

## One Person Company limitation
Section 122(1) expressly provides that sections 98 and 100–111 do not apply to a One Person Company (OPC). Do not apply this section’s ordinary meeting mechanics to an OPC as if it were an ordinary company. Section 122(2)–(3) separately governs how ordinary business that would otherwise be transacted at an AGM is handled for an OPC. Confirm OPC status and apply the current section 122 procedure before advising.

sections.heading: Ordinary notice period
sections.body: The default is not less than clear 21 days’ notice in writing or through prescribed electronic mode. Apply the governing method for counting clear days and any applicable rule or exemption.

sections.heading: Shorter notice: AGM
sections.body: For an AGM, written or electronic consent must be given by not less than 95% of the members entitled to vote at it.

sections.heading: Shorter notice: other general meeting
sections.body: For a company with share capital, the consent must come from a majority in number of members entitled to vote who represent at least 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying a right to vote. Without share capital, members representing at least 95% of total voting power must consent. Count a member only for resolutions on which that member is entitled to vote.

sections.heading: Contents, recipients and omission
sections.body: The notice states place, date, day, hour and business; it goes to members, the relevant legal representative/assignee, auditors and every director. Accidental omission or non-receipt alone does not invalidate proceedings under section 101(4).

sections.heading: One Person Company limitation
sections.body: Section 122(1) disapplies sections 98 and 100–111 to an OPC. Section 122(2)–(3) supplies a separate procedure for ordinary business otherwise transacted at an AGM. Confirm whether the company is an OPC before applying this section.

sections.heading: Electronic notice: Rule 18
sections.body: For electronic notices, separately test the member/depository email record, annual opportunity to register/update an address where applicable, subject-line particulars, accessible/non-editable notice format, dispatch and failure logs, and recipient access/retention. Rule 18 is attached only from a secondary reproduction pending Gazette-primary verification.

provisions.title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 101: Notice of meeting

examples.title: AGM shorter notice
examples.body: A company proposes an AGM on shorter notice. Counsel verifies written/electronic consents from at least 95% of members entitled to vote at that AGM, alongside all other statutory and rule requirements.

examples.title: EGM test incorrectly borrowed from AGM
examples.body: For an EGM of a company with share capital, the company relies only on consent from 95% of members by headcount, without checking whether the consenting members represent a majority in number and at least 95% of voting share capital. The AGM test alone does not establish compliance.

hypotheticals.question: A company proposes an EGM on shorter notice. Members representing 96% of the voting share capital consent, but they are not a majority in number of members entitled to vote. Is the section 101 test met?
hypotheticals.analysis: For a company with share capital, section 101(1), as amended, requires both a majority in number of members entitled to vote and representation of not less than 95% of the relevant paid-up voting share capital. On the stated facts the majority-in-number limb is not met. Verify voting entitlement, form of consent and any applicable statutory exception before reaching a final advice position.

distinctions.title: Section 101 and connected meeting-compliance requirements
distinctions.right: Section 101 regulates notice and consent. Section 102 addresses information that must accompany notice for special business; section 103 separately determines whether quorum exists.

misconceptions.trap: Treating a generic Company Law procedure as sufficient without checking the words and conditions of this section.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the distinct AGM and non-AGM shorter-notice tests in section 101(1) as amended in 2017, including both limbs for companies with share capital and the resolution-specific voting entitlement proviso.

misconceptions.trap: Treating the existence of a notice, requisition, explanatory statement or attendance list as automatic proof of statutory compliance.
misconceptions.correction: Test notice contents, recipients, the correct consent threshold, form of consent and voting entitlement separately; attendance or a high share-capital percentage alone does not prove compliance.

misconceptions.misconception: Sections 100–103 apply to every company in the same way, including a One Person Company.
misconceptions.correction: Section 122(1) expressly disapplies sections 100–111 to an OPC; section 122(2)–(3) provides a separate route for ordinary business at an OPC's AGM.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What consent is required to call a general meeting on shorter notice under section 101?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: For an AGM, written/electronic consent from not less than 95% of members entitled to vote. For another general meeting, a company with share capital needs consent from a majority in number of members entitled to vote representing at least 95% of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights; a company without share capital needs consent from members holding at least 95% of exercisable voting power. Members are counted only for resolutions on which they may vote.
